node.label: Simone de Beauvoir
node.date_label: The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) · Le Deuxième Sexe (1949; English 1953) · La Vieillesse (1970)
node.description: In Le Deuxième Sexe (The Second Sex, 1949), Beauvoir argues that women’s subordination is made through historical circumstances and social meanings rather than fixed by biology. She examines how men become the human norm while women are placed as Other, and how that unequal situation limits the exercise of freedom. The book became a major resource for feminist inquiry: Michelle Perrot recalls that it directed her first research interest toward feminism. Its reception also involves substantive disagreement. Julia Kristeva challenges its simplification of Freud while recognizing shared concerns with psychosexuality. These criticisms qualify the book’s uses as a framework for women’s and gender history.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Pour une morale de l’ambiguïté / The Ethics of Ambiguity (French original 1947); L’Amérique au jour le jour (1948); Le Deuxième Sexe (1949; H. M. Parshley English translation 1953; Borde and Malovany-Chevallier US translation edition 2010); Mémoires d’une jeune fille rangée (1958); La Force de l’âge (1960); La Force des choses (1963); La Vieillesse (1970; English The Coming of Age / Old Age, 1972); Tout compte fait (1972; English All Said and Done, 1974).
node.scope_note: Selected publisher excerpts, Butler pp. 519–523, Kristeva’s opening discussion, Perrot’s interview answers, and Navarro Antolínez’s section 3 were read. Collins’s 2017 chapter was read only through its publisher summary; the Lévi-Strauss review only through its displayed opening. Beauvoir’s monographs, the rest of Butler’s essay, and the cited Freud and Lévi-Strauss books remain unread. Bibliographical and life evidence comes from the Stanford reference entry.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her review of The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949), Beauvoir praises Lévi-Strauss for renewing French sociology through an intelligible account of human institutions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read publisher opening extract of Beauvoir’s review, translated in Feminist Writings (2015), chapter spanning pp. 58–66, first four displayed paragraphs. It calls the book a “spectacular awakening” and contrasts its method with earlier French and American approaches. SEP bibliography establishes original 1949 review and Beauvoir’s authorship despite the publisher author-field error. Full review and reviewed book unread; no further claim about agreement with his kinship conclusions.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Kristeva reads The Second Sex (1949), Beauvoir objects to Freud’s systematic rejection of choice and to the absence of an originating intentionality in his account of existence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kristeva’s 2010 author-posted intervention, opening sequence before Tout compte fait, des rêves, paragraph beginning En définitive: quotes “refus systématique de l’idée de choix” and cites The Second Sex p. 88 in an unspecified edition. Read together with the preceding paragraphs acknowledging Beauvoir’s sympathy with psychosexuality. Mediated reading explicitly attributed to Kristeva; complete Beauvoir chapter and Freud originals unread. Criticism concerns this conception of agency, not a rejection of everything in psychoanalysis.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Beauvoir et la psychanalyse : un défi réciproque” (2010), Kristeva criticizes The Second Sex (1949) for simplifying Freud, including its charge that he neglected the symbolic paternal function, while recognizing Beauvoir’s closeness to Freud on psychosexuality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author-posted 2010 conference intervention, opening paragraphs beginning Il n’en reste pas moins and En définitive, before the dream section. Kristeva identifies “simplifications” while crediting Beauvoir’s kinship with Freud on psychosexuality and warning against an anachronistic prosecution. This is a qualified criticism, not wholesale repudiation. Beauvoir’s complete psychoanalysis chapter and Freud’s books unread; only Kristeva’s own argument was directly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Second Sex (1949) makes women’s historically produced position as Other an explanatory problem for women’s history, as developed in Navarro Antolínez’s historiographical reading (2015).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Navarro Antolínez, section 3, paragraphs beginning Simone de Beauvoir, por su parte and Lo importante de este estudio histórico, notes 45–52: asks “cómo la mujer ha llegado a constituirse en la otra.” Navarro distinguishes biological conditions from social destiny and explains the historical problem. Perrot’s interview provides a specific historian’s uptake. This is a theoretical contribution and named later interpretation, not a claim Beauvoir founded the entire field or that all of her historical claims are accepted. Complete The Second Sex unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Navarro Antolínez’s “De la history a la herstory” (2015) uses The Second Sex (1949), especially its relational account of woman as Other, as a resource for explaining gender as a historical category.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Navarro Antolínez, section 3, paragraphs beginning ¿Qué se puede entender por la categoría género? through Simone de Beauvoir, por su parte and final discussion of historical method, notes 45–58. Article explicitly locates Beauvoir in gender historiography while retaining limits concerning Eurocentrism and binary categories. No assertion that Beauvoir used the later technical vocabulary of gender history or that Navarro’s comparison establishes a personal Scott–Beauvoir relationship. Original Beauvoir monograph unread beyond the publisher excerpt.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Variations on Sex and Gender in Beauvoir, Wittig and Foucault’ (1985), Judith Butler draws on Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949) to examine gender as an embodied project within cultural constraints.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Jules Gleeson’s substantive account and quoted excerpts on JSTOR Daily. The passage explains Butler’s use of Beauvoir to address choice and cultural construction. This is secondary evidence; the complete 1985 and 1986 essays were not read. No claim that Beauvoir supplied Butler’s entire later theory is proposed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Develops gender as an embodied project

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘The Personal and the Political’ (1993), Dorothy Thompson criticizes Beauvoir’s model of independent intellectual lives as unavailable to people choosing children and family.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Thompson’s response in the book publisher’s authorized interview excerpt. She explicitly relates her criticism to the independent households of intellectuals and the practical demands of raising children. The passage does not identify a particular Beauvoir book, so the relationship names Thompson’s 1993 interview rather than attributing the criticism to a reading of The Second Sex. The original journal page independently confirms the title and 1993 date; its displayed opening does not contain this exchange.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions independence without provision for children

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘True Philosophers: Beauvoir and bell’ (2012), bell hooks reflects on the influence of Beauvoir’s philosophy and life on her own work and career, according to the publisher’s description.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the SUNY Press description and chapter opening displayed by JSTOR. The description expressly identifies hooks’s essay as autobiographical and about Beauvoir’s influence. The full chapter was inaccessible and remains unread. The edge records only this broad retrospective influence; no particular concept, agreement, or criticism is attributed to hooks.

proposed_edges.relationship: Looking back in 2015 on Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973), Sheila Rowbotham identifies Beauvoir’s writings as part of her intellectual formation in connecting material life with consciousness.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s first-person retrospective, including the account of the book’s composition and publication. This is an explicit statement about Rowbotham’s intellectual formation within a substantive explanation of the book’s problem, rather than an acknowledgment or an incidental citation. Beauvoir is one of several formative writers named; no exclusive debt or particular Beauvoir title is claimed. The original book was not read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Informs the study of material life and consciousness

verification.note: Read the complete publisher Summary (three numbered argumentative moves) and publication metadata, 29 July 2017.
